name: Ethnopluralism
summary: Ethnopluralism holds that humanity is a plurality of distinct peoples, each with its own culture and homeland, and that this diversity is best kept by preserving each people's identity against universalism, globalisation and mixing. Its theorists present it as a right to difference that is anti-racist because it rejects racial hierarchy, apartheid and assimilation, while favouring restrictive immigration and congruence between territory and cultural community. Scholars dispute this self-description and regard it as a culturalised form of racism.
scope: The doctrine of the right to difference as formulated by Alain de Benoist and the French New Right (Manifesto for a European Renaissance, Part III on identity, racism and immigration, with Part II on diversity and the pluriverse), as characterised by Schlembach and Joppke. Other New Right planks (economy, federal Europe, ecology, paganism, democracy theory) belong to Nouvelle Droite, which has its own entry, and are left null. Identitarian parties' practice and later Benoist statements on unmixing are noted only where scholars report them.

notes: Themes searched in the three local sources: identity, race and racism, immigration, assimilation, territory and borders, peoples' self-determination, universalism, human rights, Islam, imperialism and the world order. Government, economy, liberty, technology, ecology and means statements are left null because the sources record them as New Right (Nouvelle Droite) planks, not as ethnopluralism's own. Scholars disagree with the Manifesto on whether the doctrine entails exclusion or unmixing, hence the low-confidence and zero answers. No expulsion, endogamy-prescription or anti-Islam position is answered, since those need direct sources from identitarian parties or later Benoist works.
